issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient also directly sustained major physical injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoidance of medical cues can fit some trauma-to-a-loved-one cases, but in this profile it appears to be driven by a personal bodily injury/medical trauma theme that is otherwise unsupported except by the implausible physical-vulnerability appraisal, making this item clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

vignette:
It happened on a rainy Tuesday afternoon in late October. Sister Margaret was driving her younger brother, David, to a doctor's appointment. He had been visiting from out of town, and she had offered to take him. She remembered the way the wipers streaked across the windshield, the sound of a truck's horn, the jarring impact. Then a gap-seconds, maybe minutes-that she could never retrieve. When the world came back, David was slumped in the passenger seat, unresponsive. He died at the scene. In the months that followed, Margaret found that the accident returned to her without warning. A flash of red brake lights in her peripheral vision, the squeal of tires from a passing car, the smell of wet asphalt-any of these could suddenly drop her back into that afternoon, the memory so vivid she could feel the vibration of the steering wheel in her hands. Yet there remained that stubborn blankness, the moments she could not account for, and she became convinced that what she had done-or failed to do-in that missing interval was the reason David was gone. If only she had checked the rearview mirror differently, if only she had not answered her phone when it buzzed, if only she had been more alert. The thought settled in her chest like a stone: I should have protected him. I failed.

That belief began to govern her days. Margaret, a nun who had taught third grade at St. Brigid's for nearly twenty years, started taking a different route to the school to avoid the intersection where the accident occurred. She stopped driving altogether when possible, asking another sister to run errands. At night, alone in her small room, she recited a specific sequence of prayers-three Hail Marys, then a decade of the Rosary, then three more-in the exact order she had said them the morning of the accident, believing that if she ever broke the pattern, something terrible would happen to someone else she loved. Grief reminders became landmines: she boxed up David's photo albums and put them in the basement, she left the room when his favorite song played on the radio, she avoided the church's memorial alcove where a candle had been lit in his name. These rituals and avoidances made sense to her-they felt like the only way to keep a dangerous world in check. But the very acts of avoidance seemed to sharpen the memory. Because she circled the long way to school, she passed the same fire station that had responded to the accident, and the sight of the red engine door would flash the full scene back to her. Because she refused to look at David's face in pictures, her mind had to work harder to hold onto his image, and the effort itself brought his ghost into her prayers. The mental rituals, instead of granting peace, kept the accident at the center of her thoughts; she could not finish a Rosary without counting the decades against the imagined seconds she could not remember. Each intrusive memory then renewed her conviction that she was at fault: See? You can't even control your own mind. You really can't be trusted.

Over weeks, the loop tightened. Margaret began to feel that she could not rely on herself for even small decisions-whether to take a different route, whether to answer a phone call, whether to let herself grieve without a ritual. She started arriving late to morning Mass because she had to repeat the prayer sequence if she lost count. Her fifth-grade students noticed that she had become jumpy, easily startled by a dropped book or a slamming door. The Mother Superior gently asked if she wanted to take a leave of absence, and Margaret's immediate thought was I can't even do my job anymore. I really am failing. The guilt pressed harder. She finally sought help not because she believed she deserved it, but because the weight of the mental arithmetic and the constant scanning of her surroundings had become so exhausting that she could no longer pretend it was working. What she feared most was not the memory itself, but what it said about her: that she was the kind of person who let someone die, and that no prayer, no avoidance, no amount of vigilance would ever change that truth. "That conviction itself became a trigger, pulling her back into the crash scene each time she let herself dwell on it, as though the memory existed only to prove her guilt."

violations.explanation: Nowhere in the vignette does it show that negative appraisals (e.g., 'I failed') cause the intrusive memory to occur; instead, memory triggers reappraisals or maladaptive strategies cause memory.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: Nowhere in the vignette does it show that negative appraisals (e.g., 'I failed') cause the intrusive memory to occur; instead, memory triggers reappraisals or maladaptive strategies cause memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
